title: Netherlands Seeks to Block US MATCH Act That Could Further Restrict ASML's China Business
author: Xebec
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

The Netherlands is intensifying diplomatic efforts to prevent the passage of proposed U.S. legislation that could impose additional restrictions on ASML’s semiconductor equipment business in China.

The bipartisan Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware (MATCH) Act seeks to limit China’s advanced semiconductor manufacturing capabilities by requiring U.S. allies, including the Netherlands and Japan, to strengthen their export controls or face unilateral American restrictions.

The proposed legislation could affect ASML’s immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems, which remain important to Chinese semiconductor manufacturers.

Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has emphasized that the Netherlands intends to retain independent authority over its export control policies. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten also plans to discuss the legislation directly with President Donald Trump at the upcoming G20 summit.

China remains a significant market for ASML, accounting for an expected 20% of its 2026 sales. Additional restrictions could therefore have meaningful commercial implications for the company.
Why It Matters​The dispute highlights growing tensions between national security objectives, commercial interests and technological sovereignty.

ASML occupies a unique position within the global semiconductor supply chain as the dominant supplier of advanced lithography equipment.

While the United States seeks to constrain China’s advanced semiconductor capabilities, European governments are increasingly concerned about Washington’s influence over their domestic industrial policies.

More restrictive export controls could also accelerate China's investment in domestic semiconductor manufacturing equipment, potentially creating additional long-term competition for established Western suppliers.

For the semiconductor industry, the MATCH Act introduces further uncertainty regarding equipment availability, international trade, manufacturing expansion and future investment decisions.

The legislation has not yet been enacted.

The broader question is whether semiconductor export controls can achieve national security objectives without undermining the global technology partnerships that have historically driven semiconductor innovation.
